data.title: Tesla Stock: Robotaxi and Semi Will Test Its 292.5x Valuation
data.description:
EV maker Tesla (TSLA) is moving closer to commercializing its next growth businesses, with autonomy and electric trucks emerging as the most important areas to watch. The company began Cybercab production in Texas during Q2. In addition, its Robotaxi service is active in seven major U.S. metro areas, and more details about the European launch of its Semi truck are expected in September. However, the question now is whether Tesla can turn autonomy and commercial trucks into meaningful businesses that can support its premium valuation of 292.5x.

200% short exposure to TSLA with TSLQ

Catalysts that May Push the Stock Higher

To begin with, autonomy remains the company's largest potential growth driver. Indeed, Tesla recently received approval to operate up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles in the Las Vegas area. This gives the company another large market where it can test whether its Robotaxi service can grow commercially. If Cybercab production rises and the need for human supervision falls, investors may assign more value to Tesla's AI and robotaxi business.

At the same time, Tesla could also see growth from its Semi. For instance, freight-tech company Einride (ENRD) plans to add 500 Tesla Semis to its North American fleet over the next two years. Tesla also plans to share European Semi specifications and launch details at the IAA Transportation show in September. That could help Tesla reach commercial customers outside the U.S. as Semi production increases in Nevada.

Meanwhile, Tesla's existing businesses provide important support. The company delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2 2026 and deployed 13.5 GWh of energy storage, which allowed revenue to reach $28.24 billion. As a result, Tesla has a large operating base that can help fund Robotaxis and Semis.

Risks to Watch Out For

However, the main risk is that Tesla is spending heavily before these projects have proven they can produce meaningful profits. Free cash flow was negative $1.1 billion in Q2 as capital spending climbed to about $5.8 billion. Tesla still held $43.52 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of June, so near-term liquidity is not the main concern. Instead, investors need to see enough future returns from that spending.

Regulation also remains important. Tesla is recalling 2.98 million vehicles in China over emergency door-release concerns. Many fixes can be delivered through software updates, which should reduce repair costs. Even so, the size of the recall shows the kind of impact that regulatory pressures can create. This will be especially true as Tesla tries to expand driverless vehicles.

Indeed, a driverless Robotaxi recently drove through a row of plastic posts in Austin. Since the Cybercab has no steering wheel or pedals, each mistake made by Tesla's current Robotaxi fleet could draw extra attention, which could impact consumer and regulatory perceptions of the service. This would likely hurt Tesla's ability to support its premium valuation.

data.title: Apple (AAPL) Lays Off Over 200 Employees as It Refocuses on AI and New Devices
data.description:
Apple (AAPL) is cutting more than 200 jobs across teams tied to Siri and the Vision Pro headset as it shifts resources toward new devices and stronger AI features, Bloomberg reported. The iPhone maker is also reducing headcount in its Intelligent Systems Experience team, which helps build AI features across its devices.

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

About 100 roles were cut from the Vision Pro department. Apple is winding down a Vision Pro team focused on making games for the headset and trimming the group that makes immersive video for the device. Another 100 jobs were cut from Siri and software teams.

While the changes will reportedly remove some roles, it will also create new ones. The affected employees will be able to apply for other jobs inside the company.

Apple Shifts Focus Toward AI and Smart Glasses

It is worth noting that the job cuts are part of a wider reshuffle across Apple's main hardware and software groups, aimed at improving efficiency and better matching customer usage patterns.

The cuts to the Siri and Intelligent Systems Experience teams are tied to a shift toward a new technical setup for an upgraded, AI‑powered version of the assistant. This change requires different engineering skills. In the Vision Pro group, Apple is scaling back its in‑house immersive content creation as the current user base is too small, making millions of dollars in production costs difficult to sustain.

At the same time, resources are moving heavily toward AI‑enabled smart glasses, expected around 2027. These glasses will use cameras, Siri, and visual intelligence tools instead of a full, power‑hungry AR display.

Apple Nears CEO Transition

Apple is getting closer to its CEO handoff. Tim Cook will step down on September 1 to become Executive Chairman, and John Ternus, Apple's Senior VP of Hardware Engineering, will move into the CEO role.

Ahead of this change, BofA analyst Wamsi Mohan said that under Cook, Apple built huge value by growing its device base, boosting services, tightening privacy, and rolling out steady, scaled innovation. He expects incoming Ternus to keep this core plan in place, with more gains coming from on‑device AI, new products, strong capital returns, and fresh markets. Mohan kept his Buy rating and $380 price target on AAPL stock.

data.title: Paramount Skydance (NASDAQ:PSKY) Stock Notches Up as Austin Makes the Short List
data.description:
Entertainment giant Paramount Skydance (PSKY) may be moving out of California, and we know that Tennessee seemed to be high on the list of potential candidates to serve as Paramount's new home base. But other states are also in the running, and Texas seems to have made the list as well. Paramount is considering Austin for its move as well. The news was mildly interesting to investors, who gave Paramount shares a fractional boost in the closing minutes of Friday's trading. Paramount has seen a 35.69% loss in its share price over the past year.

Previously, Texas had been mentioned in the same breath as Tennessee and Georgia, and there are even some signs that Austin may be more specifically on Paramount's mind. An incentive package seems to be awaiting Paramount already from whichever state Paramount ends up picking, which puts the ball squarely in California's court. Without investment, without mergers, that flow of movies is fundamentally threatened.

data.title: Crude Oil Prices End the Week 5% Higher as Iran Uncertainty Worsens
data.description:
The price of crude oil rose 5% over the past week as uncertainty grows about the path forward with Iran. Brent crude oil, the international standard, was trading at just under $95 a barrel on the afternoon of Aug. 21. West Texas Intermediate crude oil, the U.S. benchmark, was at nearly $87 a barrel heading into the weekend.

Crude oil prices have drifted higher over the last week after the Trump administration announced that it is ceasing military operations against Iran and will instead try to coerce Tehran with economic sanctions. The situation has left the fate of the Strait of Hormuz waterway near Iran uncertain. About one-fifth (20%) of the world's crude oil transited the Strait of Hormuz before the war between Iran and the U.S. erupted.

Inflation Impacts

Rising crude oil prices have reignited concerns that inflation in the U.S. will continue rising, pressuring the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in coming months. Concerns over rising oil prices and the impact on inflation is being partly blamed on the rise in U.S. Treasury yields over the past week. Yields on government bonds hit their highest level in 20 years as investors grew worried about geopolitics.

Crude oil prices had eased in the first two weeks of August as U.S. officials suggested a deal with Tehran was imminent. But an agreement never materialized, leaving the future of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz uncertain, with vessel traffic remaining well below pre-war levels. On Aug. 21, crude oil was headed for its second weekly rise, with some analysts saying the price could soon top $100 a barrel.

data.title: 'Buy Gold and a Bit of Bitcoin,' Says Billionaire Ray Dalio – Here's Why
data.description:
Billionaire investor Ray Dalio is warning that a U.S. debt crisis could arrive "in three years, give or take two." To prepare, the Bridgewater Associates founder said in a LinkedIn post that investors should consider "underweighting debt assets like bonds, and overweighting gold and a bit of Bitcoin." More specifically, he suggested putting 10% to 15% of their portfolios in gold. His concern is that the U.S. government is spending much more than it collects, and the cost of servicing its debt keeps rising.

Summer Sale - Claim 70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Dalio estimates that the federal government will collect about $5.5 trillion this year and spend roughly $7.5 trillion. That leaves a $2 trillion gap. On top of that, interest costs are expected to reach around $1 trillion, while approximately $10 trillion of government debt needs to be refinanced.

That refinancing becomes more expensive when bond yields rise, and it doesn't help that long-term Treasury yields have recently climbed to multiyear highs. Japan, the largest foreign holder of U.S. government debt, has also sold Treasuries as it tries to support the yen.

The U.S. Treasury has responded by increasing purchases of long-term government bonds. However, the move has provided only short-term support so far. That fits with Dalio's view that the underlying problem cannot be solved simply by supporting bond prices.

Why Dalio Thinks Gold Could Benefit

Dalio's concern is what happens if investors become less willing to finance growing government deficits. If demand for Treasury bonds falls, the government may have to offer higher interest rates to attract buyers, which would increase government costs even further. Another option would be for the Federal Reserve to print money and buy government debt. Dalio argues that this could weaken the dollar and increase inflation, which would cause gold and Bitcoin to perform relatively well.

Nevertheless, Dalio believes that the longer-term solution is to cut the U.S. budget deficit from about 6% of GDP to 3%. He says that would require lower government spending and more tax revenue. Lower interest rates could also help reduce the cost of servicing the debt. Furthermore, he warned that countries such as China and Japan face similar financial pressures.

data.title: Supreme Court Allows Trump to Build White House Ballroom
data.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump to resume construction on his controversial White House ballroom. Chief Justice John Roberts, in an order, stayed a federal district court judge's injunction, which had barred Trump from continuing construction while a lawsuit challenging the ballroom project was before the courts.

Roberts' order came on the same day the injunction was scheduled to take effect. In 2025, shortly after returning to the White House, Trump had the East Wing demolished without notifying Congress to make way for a planned, 90,000 square-foot ballroom. The National Trust for Historic Preservation is suing Trump to block the project on the grounds that Trump did not obtain the required authorization for it.

Rising Costs and Controversies

Construction of the ballroom has also proved controversial due to its ballooning costs. The Trump administration initially stated that the ballroom would cost $400 million and be funded entirely by private donations. However, the cost has since risen to $600 million and government records now state that U.S. taxpayers are expected to fund at least $300 million of the total cost.

Once completed, the ballroom is expected to be widely used to host social events and functions at the White House. Trump has said that having the ballroom at the White House is a matter of national security after a gunman crashed the White House Correspondents' Dinner held at a Washington, D.C. hotel earlier this year in an attempt to shoot the president.

data.title: XRP Is Up Over 30% in Just 3 Days – Is It Too Late to Buy?
data.description:
XRP (XRP-USD) is back on the move, climbing about 38% over the past three days as cryptocurrencies stage a broad recovery. The token has risen from near $1 on Wednesday to around $1.38 on Friday, while Bitcoin has moved from about $64,500 to above $77,000 during a similar period.

Summer Sale - Claim 70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

The rally began after the U.S. Treasury announced plans to at least double long-term bond buybacks, which initially sent yields lower and weakened the dollar while helping lift cryptocurrencies. President Donald Trump added another boost by urging Congress to pass the CLARITY Act, legislation intended to establish clearer rules for digital assets in the United States. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse attended Wednesday's White House crypto meeting, making the regulatory push particularly relevant for XRP investors. Billions of dollars in short liquidations then amplified the broader crypto rally as bearish positions were forced to close.

XRP has received additional support from stronger ETF demand during this week's recovery. Spot XRP ETFs recorded $8.16 million of net inflows during the first three trading days of the week, including $5.81 million on Tuesday alone.

That rally has delivered some much-needed relief following a difficult year for the cryptocurrency. Before the rally began, XRP was down about 46% since the start of 2026, making the three-day recovery particularly significant for investors who had watched the token lose nearly half its value.

So, following a 38% gain in only three days, is there still enough long-term upside left?

Investor Johnny Rice, a Motley Fool contributor, sees substantial risk for anyone buying with a five-year horizon. "Five years from now, in August of 2031, I think XRP will trade lower than $1," Rice wrote. His bearish outlook stems largely from a widening separation between Ripple's progress and the investment case surrounding its cryptocurrency.

Ripple has expanded its presence within financial services, yet Rice believes those achievements no longer guarantee stronger demand for the associated token. "The problem for XRP investors is that Ripple's success is no longer XRP's success," he opined. That distinction challenges a longstanding bullish thesis that greater adoption of Ripple's technology should ultimately translate into higher prices for its cryptocurrency.

One important part of Rice's argument involves Ripple USD (RLUSD), the company's dollar-backed stablecoin. RLUSD can serve as a bridge asset for transactions traditionally associated with XRP while offering banks an instrument pegged to the U.S. dollar. The investor therefore sees less reason to assume growing usage of Ripple's payment technology will automatically create substantial purchasing demand for XRP.

Rice remains unconvinced that XRP's limited supply provides enough support to overcome that problem over time. Every transaction on the XRP Ledger destroys a tiny amount of the cryptocurrency, which bulls view as a mechanism capable of reducing available supply. The investor rejects that argument, writing, "Unfortunately, the burn is too small to matter." Historical destruction levels support his concern that transaction activity removes only a minimal portion of outstanding tokens.

Still, Rice does not rule out another sizable move from current levels during periods of strong enthusiasm. "There absolutely could be another speculative rally that drives XRP's price well above where it trades today," the investor noted. However, his expectation changes when considering whether those gains can remain intact over several years, adding, "I just don't think that will last."

That distinction becomes particularly relevant following XRP's three-day surge from its recent lows. Rice believes investor enthusiasm can continue sending the cryptocurrency higher for periods, although he does not view those moves as evidence of stronger long-term value. "It's been driven, in my view, by hype — and hype is fickle," he stated.

Rice goes further than arguing investors simply missed a cheaper entry point before this week's recovery. The investor believes additional rallies remain possible while maintaining that the cryptocurrency could eventually fall below today's price. His conclusion captures that bearish view: "Ripple is becoming a more serious financial institution, but that doesn't mean XRP is becoming a better investment." data.title: Intel Stock (NASDAQ:INTC) Slips as Howard Lutnick Defends Intel Deal
data.description:
A while back, the United States government bought a substantial quantity of chip stock Intel (INTC), around 10% of the company itself. While this seems to have been a huge help for Intel, and also a huge gain for the government as the stock's value has soared in the interim, the deal also came with its share of controversy. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is now out defending the deal in court. Investors were oddly displeased with this, and sent Intel shares down nearly 2% in Friday afternoon's trading. Intel has seen a 271.49% rally in its share price over the past year.

Throw The Bum (Lawsuit) Out

Lutnick is directly asking a federal judge to toss the lawsuit that alleged corruption on the part of the United States government after taking an ownership stake in Intel. Lutnick asserted that the deal was actually authorized as part of the CHIPS Act, which allowed the government to attach conditions to funding grants that included payment "…in the form of stock and warrants." But the lawsuit alleges that Intel was "coerced" into handing over the ownership stake by the government attaching conditions to funds that were already due.

Betting Against Berkshire

Meanwhile, Tom Hayes, founder of Great Hill Capital, is taking his bets off Berkshire Hathaway ($BRK.A) and putting them on Intel and other "beaten-down equities" instead. Hayes declared that Berkshire's ability to beat the market was "done." In fact, Hayes looked for Berkshire to eventually be required to break up as a better way to explore underlying value. But Hayes already has one critical factor going for him, as he bought Intel at $19 a share, a move that now looks like an absolute win. Hayes noted that Intel's turnaround thesis made perfect sense, thanks to Intel's outsized role in national security.
